title: Marriage Health Check Assessment
changeLog: v3 Final: Scenario-based questions, non-linear scoring, relatable outcome signals, gender-aware insights with 4-way personalization, 4-phase narrative ordering.

STRONG.title: Thriving Together
STRONG.summary: Your marriage shows real vitality. Connection, trust, communication, and shared faith are actively present, not just surviving, but flourishing. This does not mean everything is perfect. It means the foundation you have built together can handle imperfection with grace.

genderTitle.male: A Husband Who Shows Up. And It Shows.
genderTitle.female: A Marriage That Reflects Your Investment

genderSummary.male: Your answers reveal a husband who is present, engaged, and growing. Your wife feels heard, valued, and safe with you—and that did not happen by accident. The areas where you scored highest are not just relationship skills. They are acts of love your wife experiences every day. Protect what you have built.
genderSummary.female: Your marriage is in a strong place, and your answers show that both of you are investing in it. The connection, communication, and trust you described do not just happen; they are the fruit of showing up consistently. Celebrate what is working while continuing to grow in the areas that have room.

STRONG.narrativeFrame: Your answers across 25 questions reveal a marriage with real warmth, trust, and depth. The strongest marriages are not the ones without problems; they are the ones that handle problems well. Yours shows signs of exactly that.

DEVELOPING.title: Good Bones, Room to Grow
DEVELOPING.summary: Your marriage has genuine strengths, but also clear areas where more intentional investment would transform good into great. You are not in crisis. You are at a growth edge. The couples who thrive are the ones who see this edge and lean into it instead of drifting past it.

genderTitle.male: Solid Ground, But Your Wife Needs More in Some Areas
genderTitle.female: A Marriage With Real Potential, And Clear Next Steps

genderSummary.male: You are a husband who cares—your answers make that clear. But caring is not the same as connecting. Some areas suggest your wife may need more emotional engagement, better conflict navigation, or deeper spiritual partnership. These are not indictments. They are invitations. The man who responds to them transforms his marriage.
genderSummary.female: Your marriage has real things worth celebrating, and your awareness of where it needs growth is itself a strength. The areas flagged below are not about blame; they are about what happens when two people stop being intentional in specific ways. Small, focused changes here can produce dramatic improvement in how your marriage feels day to day.

DEVELOPING.narrativeFrame: Your results show a marriage with genuine connection in some areas and room for deeper investment in others. Think of this as a tune-up, not a teardown. The specific areas below are where your focused attention will produce the best return.

GUARDED.title: Drifting — Attention Needed
GUARDED.summary: Your answers reveal a marriage where distance has crept in—emotionally, spiritually, or both. You may not be in crisis yet, but the trajectory concerns. The patterns showing up here do not fix themselves. They require honest conversation, intentional change, and possibly professional support.

genderTitle.male: Your Marriage Is Asking for Something You Have Not Given Yet
genderTitle.female: The Distance You Feel Is Real, And It Can Change

genderSummary.male: Husband, your answers suggest some hard truths. Your wife may not feel fully safe, heard, or pursued right now. These gaps do not make you a failure; but they do require action. The man who sees this assessment as a wake-up call and responds with humility will see his marriage transform. The one who explains it away will watch it continue to drift.
genderSummary.female: Your answers point to real pain and real distance. Whether the source is unresolved conflict, emotional withdrawal, or spiritual disconnection, the ache you are describing matters. You deserve to feel seen and valued in your marriage. The areas below show where the work needs to happen, and it needs to happen soon, before drift becomes damage.

GUARDED.narrativeFrame: Some of what showed up in your answers may be uncomfortable to see in writing. But the fact that you took this assessment and answered honestly means you care. That matters. The areas below are not just statistics; they are descriptions of what your marriage feels like right now. And they can change.

AT_RISK.title: Your Marriage Needs Urgent Attention
AT_RISK.summary: Your responses reveal a marriage in significant distress. Multiple core areas—trust, safety, connection, communication—are strained or broken. This is not the time for surface-level fixes. This is the time for honest reckoning, professional help, and courageous conversations.

genderTitle.male: This Is a Crisis, And How You Respond Defines What Comes Next
genderTitle.female: You Deserve Safety and Love, Your Marriage Needs Help Now

genderSummary.male: Brother, your answers describe a marriage under serious strain. Your wife may not feel safe, valued, or connected right now. This is not the moment for self-defense or minimizing. This is the moment for radical honesty and professional help. A marriage counselor, a pastor who knows your situation, or a trusted mentor—reach out this week. Your marriage can heal, but not without intervention.
genderSummary.female: Sister, your answers reveal a marriage that is hurting deeply. If safety is a concern, that comes first—above everything else on this page. If the pain is emotional distance, broken trust, or spiritual disconnection, know this: you are not crazy for feeling what you feel. Your experience is valid. Please reach out to a counselor, a pastor, or a trusted friend this week. You do not have to carry this alone.

AT_RISK.narrativeFrame: This result is difficult to receive. But the very fact that these patterns showed up means the truth is already surfacing. Healing begins when someone is willing to name what is really happening. The areas below are starting points, but professional support should be your first call.

insights.low: Your spouse may not feel seen or valued right now. Expressing appreciation is like oxygen for relationships—without it, marriage starves.
insights.medium: You appreciate your spouse sometimes, but they might need to hear it more consistently. Regular appreciation strengthens connection and security.
insights.high: You consistently affirm and encourage your spouse. Your words build them up and strengthen your marriage. This generosity is a gift.
insights.microStep: Tell your spouse one specific thing you appreciate about them today. Be genuine and specific.

insights.low: One or both of you may resist change or personal growth. Marriage thrives when both partners are committed to growing individually and together.
insights.medium: You're both somewhat open to growth but might resist in certain areas. Embracing growth mindset strengthens your marriage's resilience.
insights.high: You both actively invest in personal and relational growth. This commitment signals love and creates momentum for continued improvement.
insights.microStep: Identify one area where you want to grow as a spouse this quarter. Share this with your partner.

insights.low: Conflict may feel destructive or unmanageable right now. Learning healthier conflict patterns can transform these moments from threats into opportunities.
insights.medium: You can navigate some conflict but certain types or situations escalate quickly. Building skills prevents small issues from becoming big divides.
insights.high: You handle conflict constructively, staying respectful even in disagreement. This skill is one of the strongest predictors of lasting, thriving marriages.
insights.microStep: Next conflict, pause before responding. Take a breath and ask: 'What does my spouse really need from me right now?'

insights.low: You may feel disconnected or find communication difficult right now. Rebuilding connection requires intentional time and vulnerability.
insights.medium: You have a friendly connection but deeper communication could deepen intimacy. Small moments of openness create big shifts in marriages.
insights.high: Your friendship is strong and communication flows naturally. You genuinely enjoy each other's company and thoughts. This is a treasure to protect.
insights.microStep: Schedule 15 minutes this week with no phones. Ask your spouse: 'What's one thing on your mind right now?'

insights.low: Emotional distance may be significant right now. Rebuilding emotional intimacy requires vulnerability, time, and willingness from both partners.
insights.medium: You're emotionally connected in some areas but may hold back in others. Greater openness deepens your bond and strengthens resilience.
insights.high: You share deeply with each other, feeling truly known and understood. This emotional intimacy is the heartbeat of a thriving marriage.
insights.microStep: Share one fear or hope with your spouse this week. Let yourself be vulnerable and known.

insights.low: Your spouse may not feel safe sharing pain with you, or vice versa. Creating safety is foundational—it allows healing and deepens trust.
insights.medium: There's some safety but maybe not complete openness about hurt. Growing trust allows vulnerable conversations that strengthen marriage.
insights.high: Your spouse can share hurt without fear. You listen with compassion. This safety creates resilience and deepens your bond through hard seasons.
insights.microStep: Ask your spouse: 'Is there something that's been hurting you that you haven't shared?' Listen without defending.

insights.low: Faith may feel disconnected from your daily life right now. Integrating faith into everyday decisions and interactions strengthens marriage.
insights.medium: You live out some faith values but inconsistently. Greater consistency brings peace and alignment to your marriage.
insights.high: Your faith shapes how you treat each other daily. You live your values visibly. This integrity builds trust and models faith for others.
insights.microStep: Choose one faith value (kindness, patience, forgiveness) to practice intentionally with your spouse this week.

insights.low: Parenting and family leadership may be a tension point right now. A shared plan can reduce conflict and bring more peace at home.
insights.medium: You seem mostly aligned on family direction, but a few areas may still need clearer agreement. Small adjustments can make a big difference.
insights.high: Your answers suggest strong alignment on family values and a steady approach during pressure. This supports a safe and faith-filled home.
insights.microStep: Have a 15-minute ‘family vision chat’ this week: agree on one value you want your home to be known for.

insights.low: Financial disagreement may be a significant source of stress. Getting on the same page about money reduces conflict and increases peace.
insights.medium: You generally agree on finances but some tension areas remain. Clarifying goals and values around money helps alignment.
insights.high: You work together as a financial team with shared goals and values. You can discuss money without conflict. This alignment reduces major stress.
insights.microStep: Have a 20-minute money conversation: What's one financial goal you both want to work toward together?

insights.low: Physical connection may feel distant right now. Rebuilding physical affection—from hand-holding to intimacy—strengthens emotional bonds.
insights.medium: You share physical affection sometimes but it could deepen. Small gestures of touch throughout the day can reconnect you.
insights.high: Your physical affection is healthy and consistent. You feel connected through touch. This physical bond supports emotional intimacy and satisfaction.
insights.microStep: This week, initiate one gesture of physical affection (hug, kiss, hand-holding, or intimate time) with intention.

insights.low: You may lack dedicated, distraction-free time together. Regular one-on-one connection is vital for relationship health.
insights.medium: You spend time together but it could be more intentional or protected. Prioritizing quality time shows your spouse they matter.
insights.high: You consistently protect time together without distractions. You're fully present with each other. This investment strengthens your foundation.
insights.microStep: Schedule one date or uninterrupted time this week. Put phones away and truly focus on each other.

insights.low: You may struggle to reconnect after conflicts. The ability to repair and move forward is crucial for long-term marriage health.
insights.medium: You can usually patch things up but emotional reconnection could be deeper. True repair restores intimacy after rupture.
insights.high: You repair well after conflict, rebuilding emotional safety and connection. This skill is one of the strongest predictors of lasting marriage.
insights.microStep: If there's unresolved hurt from a recent conflict, initiate a repair conversation. Share how you felt and listen to them.

insights.low: Conflict may involve disrespect or contempt. Maintaining respect even during disagreement is essential for healthy marriage.
insights.medium: You're mostly respectful but sometimes lose it under pressure. Building consistency here prevents damage and maintains the relationship's foundation.
insights.high: You disagree without being disrespectful. You maintain love and respect even when frustrated. This maturity transforms conflict into growth.
insights.microStep: Next disagreement, pause if you feel disrespect rising. Take a break and return when you can engage respectfully.

dimensions.name: You Respond to Each Other's Concerns

insights.low: Your spouse may feel unheard or dismissed when they express concerns. Responsive listening builds security and shows they matter to you.
insights.medium: You listen sometimes but your spouse might need you to engage more consistently. Regular responsiveness demonstrates love and commitment.
insights.high: Your spouse knows you'll listen and take their concerns seriously. You respond with care. This responsiveness is foundational to trust.
insights.microStep: When your spouse shares a concern this week, resist the urge to fix or defend. Just listen and say: 'I hear you. Tell me more.'

dimensions.name: You Feel Safe With Each Other

insights.low: One or both of you may not feel physically or emotionally safe. Safety is non-negotiable—all other growth depends on it.
insights.medium: You generally feel safe but some situations trigger concern. Strengthening safety creates the foundation for deeper connection.
insights.high: You both feel genuinely safe—physically and emotionally. You can be yourselves without fear. This safety allows love to flourish.
insights.microStep: Ask your spouse: 'Do you feel safe with me?' Listen to their answer without defending. Take any concerns seriously.

insights.low: Your spiritual practices may feel disconnected or nonexistent. Shared faith practices create alignment and strength during hard seasons.
insights.medium: You share some spiritual practices but could strengthen them. Regular prayer, worship, or reflection together deepens spiritual connection.
insights.high: You practice faith together regularly—prayer, study, service. This spiritual partnership grounds your marriage and provides guidance.
insights.microStep: Start one shared spiritual practice this week: pray together, read Scripture together, or serve together.

insights.low: Responsibilities may feel unfairly distributed or create resentment. Working as a true team reduces burden and builds partnership.
insights.medium: You work together generally well but some imbalance may exist. Discussing expectations creates fairness and appreciation.
insights.high: You function as a true team. Responsibilities are discussed, shared, and appreciated. You each feel supported. This partnership is powerful.
insights.microStep: Discuss: What responsibility do you wish your spouse understood or helped with more? Listen to their answer.

insights.low: Trust may have been broken and needs rebuilding. Integrity in words and actions is essential for restoring trust.
insights.medium: You generally trust each other but some wariness remains. Continued consistency rebuilds full confidence.
insights.high: You trust each other deeply. Both of you follow through on commitments. Your integrity is reliable. This trust is the foundation of everything.
insights.microStep: Identify one commitment you've made to your spouse recently. Make sure you're following through consistently.

insights.low: Trust may have been damaged and repair feels difficult or impossible. With the right practices, trust can be rebuilt stronger than before.
insights.medium: You're trying to rebuild trust but the process feels unclear. Learning specific repair practices accelerates healing.
insights.high: When trust breaks, you both know how to repair it. You can apologize, listen, and rebuild. This skill makes your marriage resilient.
insights.microStep: If trust has been broken, identify one trust repair practice (honest conversation, consistency, transparency) to rebuild.

questions.text: It is Friday evening. No plans. You and your spouse have free time together. What most naturally happens?

options.text: We would probably end up talking, cooking, or finding something to enjoy. We genuinely like each other's company
options.outcomeLabel: You naturally enjoy each other

genderInsight.male: Natural connection with your wife is a gift. Many husbands underestimate how much their presence — not just their provision — matters.
genderInsight.female: The fact that you genuinely enjoy your husband's company and he yours is not something to take for granted. This connection is the heartbeat of your marriage.

options.text: We would each do our own thing, but comfortably. We are fine in parallel even if we do not plan anything together
options.outcomeLabel: You're comfortable apart, with low effort to connect

genderInsight.male: You're connected but there may be room for more intentionality. Many husbands express love through doing; your wife may need you to express it through being.
genderInsight.female: Comfortable parallel is fine sometimes, but watch for the drift. Women often feel the emotional distance before men notice it.

options.text: We would default to screens or separate routines. We do not naturally gravitate toward each other anymore
options.outcomeLabel: You're drifting into separate worlds

genderInsight.male: Drifting apart often happens slowly. Men tend to notice it later than women. If you're here, your wife has likely been feeling this for longer than you think.
genderInsight.female: If you're drifting into separate worlds, you've probably been feeling this awhile. Your awareness of it is the first step — don't ignore it.

options.text: Unstructured time together often feels awkward or tense. We are better with distractions between us
options.outcomeLabel: Unstructured time together feels awkward or tense

genderInsight.male: Discomfort in unstructured togetherness is a serious signal. Marriage needs both structured and unstructured connection. Consider what's making closeness feel unsafe.
genderInsight.female: If being together without plans feels awkward or tense, something important has been lost. This is worth addressing — with help if needed.

phase.title: Your Connection
phase.description: Let's start with the warmth and closeness between you.

questions.text: Your spouse does something small but thoughtful, like handling a chore you hate or bringing you something without being asked. What is your typical response?

options.text: I notice it and tell them specifically what I appreciated. This is part of how we love each other
options.outcomeLabel: You express specific, genuine appreciation

genderInsight.male: Specific, voiced appreciation is a language many men have to learn. Your wife doesn't just need to feel appreciated — she needs to hear it, in detail. The fact that you do this naturally is powerful.
genderInsight.female: Expressing specific gratitude creates a cycle of generosity in marriage. Your husband may not ask for encouragement, but he is deeply affected by whether you notice what he does.

options.text: I feel grateful but I do not always say it out loud. I assume they know I appreciate them
options.outcomeLabel: Love is felt but rarely expressed

genderInsight.male: Feeling grateful without saying it is the most common male pattern — and the most corrosive. Your wife cannot read your mind. Unspoken appreciation is functionally the same as no appreciation.
genderInsight.female: Assuming he knows you're grateful is a risky bet. Most husbands report feeling underappreciated — not because their wives don't feel it, but because they never hear it.

options.text: I might not even notice. We are both running on autopilot most days
options.outcomeLabel: Your marriage is running on autopilot

genderInsight.male: Autopilot means you've stopped seeing your wife's efforts. For men, this often happens when work stress dominates attention. What she does on autopilot is still a choice — noticing it costs you nothing.
genderInsight.female: Not noticing thoughtful gestures means the daily fabric of your marriage has become invisible. When appreciation dies, resentment grows in its place.

options.text: I might notice, but my first thought is about all the things they do not do. One good thing does not erase the frustration
options.outcomeLabel: Your negativity filter is active

genderInsight.male: If one good thing can't break through a negativity filter, your wife is being evaluated by a rigged system. A husband who can only see what's missing creates a wife who stops trying.
genderInsight.female: A negativity filter means you're keeping a mental ledger where debits always outweigh credits. Your husband's good moments deserve to count — otherwise why would he keep making them?

questions.text: Your spouse suggests a phone-free evening, just the two of you, no distractions. What is your honest internal response?

options.text: I would love that. We do this regularly and it always reconnects us
options.outcomeLabel: You have an established quality time rhythm

genderInsight.male: Regular phone-free connection means you've made your wife a priority, not an afterthought. Many husbands schedule everything except their marriage.
genderInsight.female: An established quality time rhythm shows intentionality. This doesn't happen by accident — it's built by two people who choose each other over convenience.

options.text: I would be open to it, but honestly we have not done that in a while. It might feel a little unfamiliar
options.outcomeLabel: You're willing but out of practice

genderInsight.male: Willing but rusty means the habit has faded. For men, this often means work or hobbies have quietly taken the time that used to belong to your wife. Rebuilding this rhythm is simpler than you think.
genderInsight.female: Out of practice doesn't mean broken — it means the rhythm needs resetting. The slight awkwardness of re-learning unstructured togetherness is temporary.

options.text: Part of me would resist. I am not sure what we would talk about for that long without something to do
options.outcomeLabel: You avoid unplanned closeness

genderInsight.male: If you're unsure what you'd talk about for a whole evening, your emotional intimacy has been replaced by functional communication — logistics, schedules, and kids. Your wife needs more than a roommate.
genderInsight.female: Resisting unstructured time together usually means something feels risky about being alone with your husband without distractions. That's important information.

options.text: That would feel stressful. Time alone together without distractions usually surfaces tension
options.outcomeLabel: Spending time together creates tension

genderInsight.male: If unstructured time surfaces tension rather than connection, something fundamental has shifted. For men, this often signals unresolved issues you've been avoiding by staying busy.
genderInsight.female: Time alone surfacing tension means the distractions have been holding something back. The tension isn't caused by the togetherness — it was already there, waiting.

questions.text: You are carrying a deep fear about your health, your future, your worth. It is late at night and your spouse is beside you. Do you share it?

options.text: Yes. My spouse is the first person I want to tell. I know they will hold it with care
options.outcomeLabel: Your spouse is your emotional safe harbor

genderInsight.male: Your wife being your emotional safe harbor means she feels trusted with your real self — not just the strong version. That trust is your marriage's greatest asset.
genderInsight.female: Being able to bring your deepest fears to your husband means you've built something rare. Protect this vulnerability — it's the foundation of everything.

options.text: Maybe parts of it. I would share enough for connection but hold back the deepest part to protect them or myself
options.outcomeLabel: You share enough for connection but hold back to protect yourself

genderInsight.male: Filtered vulnerability is common in men — sharing the 'acceptable' emotions but hiding the deeper fears. Your wife wants the real you, not the edited version.
genderInsight.female: Sharing selectively is natural but limiting. If you're holding back the hardest parts, consider what you're protecting — yourself, or the image your husband has of you.

options.text: Probably not. I do not think they would know what to do with something that heavy, or I do not want to burden them
options.outcomeLabel: You fear burdening them or assume they couldn't handle it

genderInsight.male: Protective isolation often looks like 'not wanting to burden her.' But your wife would rather carry weight with you than wonder why you're distant.
genderInsight.female: Pulling away emotionally to protect yourself makes sense — but it leaves your husband on the outside wondering what he did wrong.

options.text: No. Sharing deep fears with my spouse does not feel safe. I would call a friend or carry it alone
options.outcomeLabel: Your spouse is not your emotional safe person

genderInsight.male: If your spouse is not your emotional safe person, that's one of the most important things to address in your marriage right now.
genderInsight.female: If your husband is not who you go to with your deepest feelings, something foundational needs attention. You deserve to be fully known in your marriage.

genderVariant.male: You are carrying a deep fear about your health, your ability to provide, your worth as a man. It is late at night and your wife is beside you. Do you share it?
genderVariant.female: You are carrying a deep fear about your health, your future, something that keeps you up at night. It is late and your husband is beside you. Do you share it?

questions.text: When was the last time physical affection with your spouse, like a lingering hug, a genuine kiss, holding hands, or sexual intimacy, felt natural and wanted by both of you?

options.text: Recently and regularly. Physical connection is alive and mutual in our marriage
options.outcomeLabel: Your connection is alive and mutual

genderInsight.male: Mutual, alive physical connection means both you and your wife feel desired — not dutiful. Many husbands underestimate how much their wife's sense of being wanted shapes this dynamic.
genderInsight.female: Mutual physical connection means neither of you is performing or enduring — you're genuinely drawn to each other. This is worth actively protecting.

options.text: It happens but it takes more effort than it used to. We are not as naturally affectionate as we once were
options.outcomeLabel: You're trying hard to stay connected

genderInsight.male: Effortful but present means the desire is still there but the spontaneity has faded. For husbands, this often means the emotional connection needs rebuilding — for most women, intimacy follows feeling known.
genderInsight.female: If physical connection takes more effort, consider what's changed emotionally. For many women, physical desire follows emotional safety — if one has dropped, the other often follows.

options.text: It has been a while. Physical intimacy has become a source of tension, avoidance, or one-sidedness
options.outcomeLabel: You experience tension or avoidance around intimacy

genderInsight.male: Tension or avoidance around physical intimacy is one of the most painful markers in a marriage. For men who feel rejected, the instinct is to withdraw — but withdrawal deepens the problem.
genderInsight.female: If physical intimacy has become a source of tension, you may be caught between obligation and desire. You deserve to feel genuinely wanted, not pressured — and so does your husband.

options.text: I honestly cannot remember. We rarely touch, and when we do it feels forced or obligatory
options.outcomeLabel: You rarely touch and it feels forced or obligatory

genderInsight.male: Absent physical connection means a critical part of your marriage has gone dormant. Many husbands grieve this silently. This requires honest, possibly professional conversation — not just hope.
genderInsight.female: Forced or absent intimacy signals something significant has broken in the connection. This isn't about frequency — it's about whether you feel safe, seen, and desired. All three matter.

questions.text: Think about an ordinary week, no crisis, no special event. How does faith show up between you and your spouse day to day?

options.text: We pray together, read Scripture, or have faith conversations regularly. It is woven into our weekly rhythm
options.outcomeLabel: Your faith is woven into your weekly rhythm

genderInsight.male: Woven-in faith means you're not just a Christian husband on Sunday — you're leading spiritually in the daily. This creates a home where faith is caught, not just taught.
genderInsight.female: Regular shared spiritual practice means faith isn't just your individual pursuit — it's the connective tissue of your marriage. This shared rhythm sustains when everything else shakes.

options.text: We attend church and occasionally pray together, but our daily faith life is mostly individual
options.outcomeLabel: You attend church together but your daily faith life is mostly individual

genderInsight.male: Sunday faith without daily rhythm means your spiritual leadership is event-based, not lifestyle-based. Your wife and kids experience your faith in the Tuesday moments, not just the Sunday ones.
genderInsight.female: Church attendance without daily shared practice means your marriage's spiritual foundation is thinner than it looks. It may hold during calm seasons but buckle under pressure.

options.text: One of us is more spiritually active than the other. We do not share a common faith rhythm
options.outcomeLabel: Only one of you is pursuing spiritual growth

genderInsight.male: If your wife carries the spiritual effort alone, she feels spiritually lonely in her own marriage. A husband who leads spiritually isn't one who has all the answers — he's one who shows up.
genderInsight.female: One-sided spiritual effort is exhausting. If you're the one always initiating prayer or faith conversations, it may feel like you're dragging your husband toward God rather than walking together.

options.text: Faith is not part of our daily life as a couple. We rarely pray, read, or talk about God together
options.outcomeLabel: Your faith is absent from daily life together

genderInsight.male: A marriage without shared faith practice is building on sand during storms. As a husband, initiating even one small spiritual practice — a weekly prayer, a dinner blessing — changes the direction.
genderInsight.female: Faith absent from your daily life together means you're navigating marriage with human resources alone. In hard seasons, this absence is felt most acutely.

questions.text: You and your spouse disagree about something that matters to both of you, not a small thing. What most often happens in the first 10 minutes?

options.text: We express our views, listen to each other, and look for understanding. It is tense but productive
options.outcomeLabel: You manage tension productively

genderInsight.male: Managing perpetual issues with respect rather than needing to 'win' is a sign of real maturity. Many men struggle to accept that not every problem has a solution.
genderInsight.female: Your ability to sit in unresolved tension without jumping to worst-case thinking shows deep relational strength. Not everything needs to be fixed — some things just need to be held.

options.text: We start okay but one or both of us gets emotional. It takes effort to stay on track
options.outcomeLabel: Emotions take over in your discussions

genderInsight.male: Emotions interrupting good intentions is human. For men, this often looks like frustration escalating into silence or sharpness. Name the emotion before it drives the response.
genderInsight.female: When emotions take over, it's usually because something deeper got touched. Learning to name the real feeling underneath — not just the surface anger — changes everything.

options.text: One of us shuts down or walks away. We do not know how to stay in the hard conversation
options.outcomeLabel: You leave conversations before resolution

genderInsight.male: Premature exit from conflict is the most common male pattern in marriage. Your wife experiences your withdrawal as abandonment, even if you call it 'cooling off.'
genderInsight.female: Avoiding the issue feels like peace, but it's actually distance. The unresolved thing doesn't go away — it just waits for a worse moment to resurface.

options.text: It escalates quickly. Voices raise, words get sharp, and we end up further apart than when we started
options.outcomeLabel: Conflict escalates quickly with sharp words and distance

genderInsight.male: Premature exit from conflict is the most common male pattern in marriage. Your wife experiences your withdrawal as abandonment, even if you call it 'cooling off.'
genderInsight.female: Avoiding the issue feels like peace, but it's actually distance. The unresolved thing doesn't go away — it just waits for a worse moment to resurface.

phase.title: Your Conflicts
phase.description: Now let's explore how you handle tension and repair.

questions.text: During an argument, your spouse says something that really gets under your skin. It feels unfair and personal. What comes out of your mouth next?

options.text: A breath first, then I ask that we slow down so I don't say something I will regret
options.outcomeLabel: You hold the line on respect

genderInsight.male: Holding the line on respect when your wife hits below the belt is the hardest test of self-control a man faces. Your restraint in this moment builds more trust than a thousand good days.
genderInsight.female: Pausing when your husband provokes you shows the kind of emotional discipline that transforms arguments from destructive to productive. This restraint is a gift to your marriage.

options.text: I try to stay calm but my tone probably shifts. I might say something sharp before I catch myself
options.outcomeLabel: Your tone shifts under pressure but you catch yourself quickly

genderInsight.male: Tone shifts under pressure are human. The key for husbands is catching the sharp word quickly and naming it: 'That came out wrong. Let me try again.' Repair speed matters more than perfection.
genderInsight.female: Slipping under pressure then catching yourself shows growth. The gap between the slip and the repair is where your marriage either spirals or stabilizes.

options.text: Match energy. If they come at me with heat, they are going to get it back. That is just how it goes
options.outcomeLabel: You match their intensity if they come at you with heat

genderInsight.male: Matching your wife's energy in a fight means neither of you is regulating — you're both escalating. As a husband, someone has to break the cycle. That's not weakness; it's leadership.
genderInsight.female: Fire meeting fire feels justified in the moment but leaves both of you burned. One of you has to choose de-escalation — and it can start with you.

options.text: I go for the jugular. When I am hurt, I know exactly what words will hurt them back
options.outcomeLabel: You go for the weak spot

genderInsight.male: Going for the jugular means you've weaponized your knowledge of your wife's vulnerabilities. This is one of the most damaging things a husband can do — it turns intimacy into ammunition.
genderInsight.female: Using your knowledge of his weak spots as a weapon turns the safest relationship into the most dangerous one. This pattern erodes trust at a level that's very hard to rebuild.

genderVariant.male: During an argument, your wife says something that really gets under your skin. She knows exactly where you are vulnerable. In that heated moment, what do you do?
genderVariant.female: During an argument, your husband says something that really gets under your skin. He knows exactly where you are vulnerable. In that heated moment, what do you do?

questions.text: After a painful argument last night, you wake up the next morning. Your spouse is already up. What typically happens?

options.text: One of us reaches out with a touch, a soft word, or an apology. We both want to repair and we know how
options.outcomeLabel: You have a natural repair instinct

genderInsight.male: Initiating repair the next morning shows relational courage. Many husbands wait for their wives to make the first move — your willingness to reach across the tension is what safe marriages are built on.
genderInsight.female: Natural repair instinct means you or your husband breaks the ice without either of you needing to 'lose.' This capacity for reconnection is one of the strongest predictors of marriage longevity.

options.text: We are polite but distant. It takes us a few hours or a day before we can really talk about it
options.outcomeLabel: You're polite but distant until you can really talk

genderInsight.male: A slow thaw is better than a freeze. The risk for husbands is letting 'a few hours' become a few days. Don't wait for the perfect moment — reach out imperfectly.
genderInsight.female: Politeness masking distance is a common post-fight pattern. The real repair happens when someone moves past polite and into honest. Don't wait for him — go first.

options.text: We act like it did not happen. Life resumes, but the unresolved tension sits underneath everything
options.outcomeLabel: You avoid repairing

genderInsight.male: Pretending the fight didn't happen is how unresolved issues accumulate in marriage. Husbands who avoid repair conversations create wives who stop bringing up problems altogether.
genderInsight.female: Acting like nothing happened protects the peace but stores the poison. Each unaddressed argument adds weight to the next one — until a small trigger causes a massive reaction.

options.text: The coldness continues, sometimes for days. Neither of us knows how to break the silence
options.outcomeLabel: You experience prolonged disconnection

genderInsight.male: Multi-day coldness after arguments means your marriage lacks a repair mechanism. For husbands, learning to break the silence — even clumsily — is one of the most important skills you can build.
genderInsight.female: Prolonged disconnection after conflict means neither of you knows how to bridge the gap. This pattern doesn't improve with time — it requires learning new tools for reconnection.

questions.text:
Your spouse sits you down and says: "There is something I have been wanting to talk to you about. It has been bothering me."
What happens in your body and mind first?

options.text: I turn toward them and listen. If something is bothering them, I want to know
options.outcomeLabel: You turn toward your spouse's concern

genderInsight.male: Turning toward your wife's concern without defensiveness creates safety for honesty. Many wives stop sharing concerns because their husbands' first reaction is self-protection. Your openness is a gift.
genderInsight.female: Genuine curiosity when your husband brings something up shows emotional maturity. Many husbands hesitate to raise concerns — your receptiveness encourages his honesty.

options.text: Listening, but my guard goes up. Hoping this is not about something I did wrong
options.outcomeLabel: Your guard goes up and you hope it's not about you

genderInsight.male: Guard going up when your wife says 'we need to talk' is common in men who associate feedback with failure. Learning to separate 'she has a concern' from 'I'm not enough' changes everything.
genderInsight.female: Defensiveness before he even finishes often comes from anticipating criticism. Try receiving the concern as information, not an attack — it usually shifts the entire conversation.

options.text: I brace myself. Conversations that start this way usually end in me feeling blamed or criticized
options.outcomeLabel: You brace yourself and expect to feel blamed or criticized

genderInsight.male: Bracing for attack means your wife's attempts to share have historically felt like blame sessions. Either the pattern of how she raises things needs work, or your interpretation of concern as criticism does — probably both.
genderInsight.female: If your husband raising a concern feels like being put on trial, something has gone wrong in how you both communicate. You deserve to hear concerns without feeling attacked — and so does he.

options.text: Irritation before they even finish. Already feeling like whatever it is, I am not enough
options.outcomeLabel: You feel irritation and inadequacy before they even finish

genderInsight.male: automatic shutdown means your wife can't reach you with anything that sounds remotely like dissatisfaction. This makes honest marriage impossible — she'll either stop trying or start hiding.
genderInsight.female: Irritation before the conversation even starts means you've already decided what he's going to say — and it's nothing good. This automatic defense closes the door on genuine dialogue.

questions.text: Your spouse wrongs you, not a small thing. You know as a Christian you are called to forgive. Three weeks later, what is the honest state of your heart?

options.text: The bitterness is loosening. Not perfectly gone, but I am choosing forgiveness daily and the freedom is growing. It is a process, not a switch
options.outcomeLabel: You practice active forgiveness

genderInsight.male: Active forgiveness as a daily practice — not a one-time declaration — shows spiritual maturity that will sustain your marriage through far worse offenses than this one.
genderInsight.female: Releasing bitterness daily rather than just deciding to forgive once shows you understand that forgiveness is a process, not an event. This depth protects your heart and your marriage.

options.text: I have chosen to forgive but the hurt still surfaces. I keep bringing it back to God because my flesh wants to hold on
options.outcomeLabel: You choose forgiveness daily

genderInsight.male: Choosing forgiveness while the hurt still surfaces is honest faith in action. Many men think forgiveness means the pain stops — it doesn't. It means you stop weaponizing it.
genderInsight.female: Daily choosing forgiveness while still feeling the ache is one of the hardest things faith asks of a wife. Your persistence in this shows genuine spiritual depth.

options.text: I spoke forgiveness, but emotional distance has crept in—self-protection wearing a forgiveness mask
options.outcomeLabel: You say you forgive, but your heart stays guarded

genderInsight.male: Verbal forgiveness with emotional distance is a common male pattern — 'I said I forgive you, why are we still talking about it?' But your wife can feel the wall, even when you can't see it.
genderInsight.female: Saying forgiveness while maintaining protective distance means the hurt is still running the show. Your husband may think things are resolved while you're quietly keeping him at arm's length.

options.text: Still carrying it, and part of me feels justified, even though I know Scripture says otherwise
options.outcomeLabel: You feel justified in your bitterness

genderInsight.male: Justified bitterness is still bitterness — and it corrodes marriage from the inside. As a husband, carrying resentment doesn't punish your wife; it poisons you and everything you touch.
genderInsight.female: Holding onto the wrong because it feels deserved is understandable — but bitterness doesn't hurt the person who wronged you. It hurts you, and it hurts the marriage.

questions.text: You discover your spouse told a small lie about something. Nothing major, but they clearly hid the truth. What does this bring up for you?

options.text: I bring it up directly. Small lies matter to me, but I trust our foundation enough to address it without spiraling
options.outcomeLabel: You address issues directly from a foundation of trust

genderInsight.male: Addressing dishonesty directly from a foundation of trust shows a marriage with strong bones. Protect this by continuing to choose transparency even when it's costly.
genderInsight.female: Your trust foundation is solid. Keep choosing honesty over comfort — even about the small things.

options.text: It bothers me and I will bring it up, but part of me wonders what else they might be hiding. One lie opens a door
options.outcomeLabel: One lie has opened a door of lasting doubt

genderInsight.male: One lie triggering constant watchfulness often reflects past wounds — either in this marriage or before it. Address the pattern, not just the incident.
genderInsight.female: If one small lie opens a flood of doubt, there may be older trust wounds at play. Consider whether this reaction is proportional or historical.

options.text: It confirms what I already suspected. Trust has been shaky for a while and this adds to the pattern
options.outcomeLabel: You experience a pattern of trust erosion

genderInsight.male: Trust erosion in marriage is often slow — small lies, partial truths, managed stories. Each one feels minor. Together they hollow out the foundation.
genderInsight.female: If you can see a pattern of erosion, you're already past the 'one-time thing' stage. This needs direct conversation — or professional help.

options.text: I am not surprised. Dishonesty has become normal between us and I am not sure it can change
options.outcomeLabel: Dishonesty has become normal between you

genderInsight.male: Normalized dishonesty means the marriage has adapted to untruth. This requires serious intervention — not just a conversation, but likely professional help.
genderInsight.female: When dishonesty becomes normal, the relationship loses its ability to self-correct. This is urgent and worth professional support.

questions.text: Something your spouse did genuinely hurt you, not on purpose, but the pain is real. You need to tell them. What do you expect will happen when you do?

options.text: They will listen, take it seriously, and care about how I feel, even if they see it differently
options.outcomeLabel: You expect care and receptivity

genderInsight.male: Expecting care when you share hurt means your wife has built trust that vulnerability is safe with her. Protect this by continuing to bring things to her rather than handling them alone.
genderInsight.female: Knowing your husband will receive your hurt with care rather than defensiveness is one of the most important safety markers in a marriage. This trust took work — honor it.

options.text: They will probably listen, but they might get defensive at first before they really hear me
options.outcomeLabel: You're safe sometimes, defended against other times

genderInsight.male: Expecting initial defensiveness before real listening suggests a pattern you've both adapted to. As a husband, consider whether you do the same when she shares — often the pattern is mutual.
genderInsight.female: If sharing hurt usually starts with his defensiveness, you've learned to brace for it. But notice whether the eventual listening is genuine — if so, the pattern is workable, just uncomfortable.

options.text: They will likely turn it around on me or explain why I should not feel that way
options.outcomeLabel: You expect dismissal or reversal

genderInsight.male: Expecting dismissal or reversal means sharing your hurt has historically been met with 'you shouldn't feel that way' or 'what about what you did?' This makes emotional intimacy impossible.
genderInsight.female: If you expect him to turn it around on you, you've been conditioned to believe your feelings are invalid in this relationship. That conditioning isn't truth — it's damage.

options.text: Silence. The last few times I tried to share, it made things worse. So I carry it alone now, which feels lonely but safer
options.outcomeLabel: You've learned silence from repeated pain

genderInsight.male: Learned silence — choosing not to share because sharing made things worse — is one of the saddest patterns in marriage. Your hurt doesn't disappear because you stop voicing it; it just goes underground.
genderInsight.female: Giving up on sharing hurt because it always backfires means you've lost the most basic safety in your marriage. This isn't something you can fix alone — please consider professional help.

phase.title: Your Trust
phase.description: This section probes the deeper layers — safety, honesty, and vulnerability.

genderVariant.male: Something your wife did genuinely hurt you, not on purpose, but the pain is real. You are deciding whether to tell her. What determines your decision?
genderVariant.female: Something your husband did genuinely hurt you, not on purpose, but the pain is real. You are deciding whether to tell him. What determines your decision?

questions.text: Your spouse broke a commitment that mattered to you. They apologize sincerely. A week later, what does the trust-rebuilding process actually look like?

options.text: We talked about what happened, what needs to change, and we check in on progress. It is painful but we face it together
options.outcomeLabel: You have a structured, intentional repair process

genderInsight.male: Structured repair with accountability shows your marriage has a system for rebuilding trust, not just hoping the apology is enough. Many husbands apologize and expect that to close the book — real repair is a process.
genderInsight.female: A clear repair process means trust isn't left to chance after a breach. This structure protects both of you — he knows what's expected, and you know what progress looks like.

options.text: The apology helped but we have not really talked about what needs to change. I am watching to see if their behavior shifts
options.outcomeLabel: You hope for change without a plan

genderInsight.male: Watching without a plan means you've accepted the apology but not established what change looks like. As a husband, either ask your wife what she needs, or name what you'll do differently.
genderInsight.female: Watching for change without a roadmap keeps you in evaluation mode rather than partnership mode. Consider naming what rebuilding looks like rather than silently monitoring.

options.text: We moved on from it but I still feel it. The apology did not actually address the root issue
options.outcomeLabel: You apologize but don't make real changes

genderInsight.male: A surface apology without addressing the root means the same commitment will likely be broken again. As a husband, if your apology doesn't include a plan for change, it's just damage control.
genderInsight.female: If his apology felt sincere but nothing structural changed, you're right to feel unsatisfied. Real repair addresses the WHY behind the breach, not just the WHAT.

options.text: This has happened before and the pattern repeats. Apology, temporary change, then back to the same behavior
options.outcomeLabel: You experience a cyclical breach pattern

genderInsight.male: A cyclical breach pattern — apologize, improve briefly, repeat — means the apology itself has lost credibility. Your wife no longer trusts your words. Only sustained changed behavior can rebuild this.
genderInsight.female: Recurring breach and apology cycles train you to distrust his promises, no matter how sincere they sound. This pattern requires professional intervention — you can't fix a loop from inside it.

questions.text:
Your spouse tells you: "I think we should see a marriage counselor, not because we are in crisis, but because I want us to keep growing."
What is your honest reaction?

options.text: I would be open and even encouraged. Investing in growth before crisis shows wisdom
options.outcomeLabel: You have a proactive growth mindset

genderInsight.male: Welcoming proactive counseling shows your wife that you value the marriage enough to invest before crisis. Many men only consider counseling when things are already breaking — your openness sets you apart.
genderInsight.female: Being encouraged by a counseling suggestion means you see growth as a shared project, not a sign of failure. This mindset is the difference between marriages that stagnate and marriages that deepen.

options.text: I would be willing but a little uncomfortable. I associate counseling with problems, not growth
options.outcomeLabel: You're open but uncomfortable

genderInsight.male: Willingness with discomfort is honest. Many men associate counseling with admitting failure. Reframe it: counseling is how strong marriages stay strong — like maintenance on a house, not emergency repair.
genderInsight.female: Discomfort with counseling is normal — it's vulnerable work. The fact that you'd still go despite the discomfort shows your commitment to the marriage outweighs your self-protection.

options.text: Defensive. If they think we need counseling, they must think something is seriously wrong
options.outcomeLabel: You get defensive when growth is suggested

genderInsight.male: Defensiveness about counseling often comes from a man's belief that he should be able to fix things himself. But marriage isn't a solo project, and outside perspective isn't an indictment of your leadership.
genderInsight.female: If your husband's suggestion of counseling makes you feel something is wrong with you, consider that he might be investing rather than criticizing. The interpretation you choose shapes your response.

options.text: Resistance. We should be able to figure things out on our own without bringing in an outsider
options.outcomeLabel: You're closed to outside advice or growth

genderInsight.male: Resistance to outside help is one of the strongest predictors of eventual marriage failure. Believing you 'should be able to figure it out' puts an impossible burden on two imperfect people.
genderInsight.female: Refusing outside help means the marriage only has the tools it already has — which are the same tools that created the current problems. Growth requires something new.

questions.text: There is one issue in your marriage that keeps coming back. You have argued about it multiple times and it never fully resolves. What is the current state of that issue?

options.text: We have accepted we see it differently and found a way to live with the tension. Not everything has to be solved, just managed with respect
options.outcomeLabel: You manage recurring issues with respect

genderInsight.male: Accepting that some issues won't fully resolve — and managing them with respect — is advanced marital skill. Many husbands need to 'win' or 'fix' every disagreement. Your ability to live in productive tension shows real maturity.
genderInsight.female: Living with an unresolved issue without it poisoning the marriage is one of the hardest things marriage asks. Your ability to hold the tension while maintaining connection shows deep relational strength.

options.text: We revisit it occasionally and make small progress. It is still tender but we are learning to talk about it better
options.outcomeLabel: You're slowly improving on hard topics

genderInsight.male: Slow progress on a recurring issue is still progress. For husbands, the temptation is to declare the issue 'dealt with' after one good conversation. Recurring issues need recurring attention — not a one-time fix.
genderInsight.female: Small progress on a recurring issue shows both of you are still engaged with it. The danger isn't the issue itself — it's the temptation to stop trying because the progress feels too slow.

options.text: We avoid it now. Bringing it up always leads to the same fight, so we have an unspoken agreement to steer clear
options.outcomeLabel: You avoid the recurring issue

genderInsight.male: Avoiding a recurring issue by unspoken agreement creates a no-go zone in your marriage. As a husband, the issue you both refuse to discuss becomes the thing that silently controls the relationship.
genderInsight.female: An unspoken agreement to avoid the hard topic protects the peace but starves the marriage. The issue doesn't go away — it just operates underground, influencing moods and reactions you can't trace.

options.text: It poisons everything. Even when we are not talking about it, it sits under the surface and affects how we relate
options.outcomeLabel: An unresolved issue poisons your relationship

genderInsight.male: Rapid escalation or toxic avoidance are both marriage-threatening patterns. This is the area with the highest return on investment for counseling.
genderInsight.female: If conflict has become poisonous or absent in your marriage, this needs professional attention. The patterns here don't improve on their own.

questions.text: When your spouse is truly angry, not just frustrated, how does your body respond?

options.text: I feel calm enough to engage. Their anger does not make me feel unsafe, just alert that something matters to them
options.outcomeLabel: You feel safe even when your spouse is angry

genderInsight.male: Feeling safe even when your spouse is angry means anger is expressed without threat. This is what healthy homes look like.
genderInsight.female: Feeling safe when your husband is angry means his anger doesn't threaten your sense of security. This is foundational.

options.text: Tense and cautious, watching my words carefully to avoid making it worse
options.outcomeLabel: You're walking on eggshells

genderInsight.male: Walking on eggshells around your wife's anger may feel like 'keeping the peace' — but it's actually a sign that emotional safety needs work.
genderInsight.female: Walking on eggshells means you're managing his emotions instead of living freely in your own home. This deserves attention.

options.text: Afraid. Their anger scares me and my body either freezes, flees, or tries to make it stop as fast as possible
options.outcomeLabel: Your fear response gets activated

genderInsight.male: A fear response to your spouse's anger is a significant warning. This may indicate patterns that need professional help to address safely.
genderInsight.female: If your body responds with fear to your husband's anger, that is your body telling you something important. Please listen to it.

options.text: Physically unsafe. Their anger has included intimidation, breaking things, blocking exits, or physical aggression. This is not normal and it is not your fault
options.outcomeLabel: Physical safety is threatened — urgent support needed

genderInsight.male: If you feel physically unsafe when your spouse is angry, this is not a counseling issue — this is a safety issue. Please reach out to a pastor, trusted friend, or professional immediately.
genderInsight.female: If your husband's anger makes you fear for your physical safety, please reach out for help. This is not something to manage alone. You deserve to be safe.

questions.text: Your spouse asks you about something you would rather not share: a purchase, a conversation, or how you spent your time. You know the full truth might cause tension. What do you do?

options.text: The truth, even the uncomfortable parts. Transparency matters more to me than avoiding a hard moment
options.outcomeLabel: You choose transparency over comfort

genderInsight.male: Choosing truth over comfort — even when you know it might cause tension — shows your marriage is built on honesty rather than image management. As a husband, this transparency is what makes your wife feel safe.
genderInsight.female: Being willing to share the uncomfortable truth rather than managing the narrative means you trust the marriage to handle honesty. This kind of courage from a wife builds the deepest kind of trust.

options.text: I tell the truth but I soften it. I share the facts without all the details that might hurt
options.outcomeLabel: You're truthful but filter the hard parts

genderInsight.male: Sharing truth but softening it is often a sign of emotional maturity, not dishonesty. The key question for husbands: are you softening to protect her feelings, or to protect yourself from her reaction?
genderInsight.female: Filtering truth to make it gentler shows care for your husband's feelings. Just make sure the filtering doesn't remove the actual substance — 'softened truth' is still truth. 'Curated truth' is not.

options.text: Deflection or minimizing. Answering without technically lying, but leaving out the parts that would cause problems
options.outcomeLabel: You withhold important truths

genderInsight.male: Omitting uncomfortable details feels like 'not lying' but functions the same way. As a husband, what you withhold shapes your wife's reality just as much as what you say. Managed truth erodes the same as outright dishonesty.
genderInsight.female: Deflecting or minimizing when asked a direct question is a form of dishonesty that doesn't feel like lying. But your husband made a direct ask — and you chose to answer a different question.

options.text: I have lied in situations like this before. Sometimes it feels easier to manage the story than face the fallout
options.outcomeLabel: You control the narrative to avoid conflict

genderInsight.male: If you've lied to manage your wife's perception, you've chosen control over intimacy. Every lie — even a small one — teaches your wife that the version of you she sees isn't real. Rebuilding from this requires painful honesty.
genderInsight.female: Managing the story rather than telling the truth means you've decided what your husband can handle. But that's not your decision to make — and the lie itself does more damage than the truth would have.

questions.text: It is a chaotic week. The house is a mess, the kids need attention, work is demanding, errands are piling up. How does the load get distributed between you and your spouse?

options.text: We check in with each other, divide and conquer, and neither of us keeps score. We are a team
options.outcomeLabel: You work together fluidly, without keeping score

genderInsight.male: Score-free teamwork means neither of you is keeping a ledger. In many marriages, men underestimate the invisible labor their wives carry. That you don't — that's real partnership.
genderInsight.female: Fluid teamwork means the household runs on partnership, not scorekeeping. If you're here, you and your husband have built something many couples struggle to find.

options.text: We manage, but one of us usually carries more and it creates quiet frustration
options.outcomeLabel: There's an unspoken imbalance in responsibilities

genderInsight.male: Unspoken imbalance is extremely common — and many men are often unaware of it. The work you don't see is still being done by someone.
genderInsight.female: You may be carrying more than your husband realizes. The question isn't whose fault it is — it's whether you can talk about it without it becoming a fight.

options.text: It is mostly on one person, and the resentment is building
options.outcomeLabel: Visible resentment comes from unfair division

genderInsight.male: Visible resentment around household labor often reflects a deeper issue — feeling unseen or undervalued. This is about more than chores.
genderInsight.female: Resentment about imbalance is rarely just about the dishes. It's about feeling like a partner vs. Feeling like a manager. Name the real issue.

options.text: Weeks like this turn into full-blown conflict. Responsibilities are a constant battle in our home
options.outcomeLabel: Household duties keep causing conflict

genderInsight.male: When responsibilities become a recurring source of conflict, it usually means the partnership has broken down into scorekeeping. This needs restructuring, not just redistribution.
genderInsight.female: If every week feels like a battle over who does what, the marriage has a teamwork problem that goes deeper than task allocation.

phase.title: Your Future Together
phase.description: Finally, let's look at how you build together as a team.

questions.text: Your spouse makes a significant purchase without discussing it with you first. When you find out, what happens?

options.text: We talk about it. We have agreed on how we handle money and if one of us goes outside that, we address it respectfully
options.outcomeLabel: You have a clear shared financial framework

genderInsight.male: A clear shared financial framework means money isn't a power tool in your marriage. Many husbands and wives struggle with financial control dynamics — your transparency protects the partnership.
genderInsight.female: Agreed-upon financial boundaries mean purchases don't become betrayals. This framework only works if both of you actually follow it — and both feel equally empowered in financial decisions.

options.text: I feel uneasy and bring it up, but we do not have a clear system so the conversation is messy
options.outcomeLabel: You have no shared plan for finances

genderInsight.male: No clear financial system means every purchase becomes a negotiation. As a husband, initiating a money conversation — boundaries, thresholds, shared accounts — is an act of leadership.
genderInsight.female: Messy financial conversations often reflect deeper issues — control, trust, or different values around money. Creating a system together removes the emotion from individual purchases.

options.text: I am upset but I might not say anything. Money conversations between us always end badly
options.outcomeLabel: You avoid talking about money

genderInsight.male: Avoiding money conversations because they always end badly means financial decisions are made by default rather than by agreement. Husbands often either over-control or completely withdraw from finances — neither works.
genderInsight.female: If money talks always end in conflict, there may be an underlying trust or control issue that the financial disagreement is just surfacing. Addressing the real issue unlocks the money conversation.

options.text: This kind of thing happens often and it always leads to a blowup. We cannot talk about money without fighting
options.outcomeLabel: You have ongoing conflict about money

genderInsight.male: Chronic financial conflict often reflects a deeper power struggle. As a husband, financial transparency isn't just practical — it's a trust issue. Secretive spending erodes marriage faster than debt itself.
genderInsight.female: Money being an untouchable topic in your marriage means one of the most practical areas of partnership is completely broken. This rarely improves without structured help.

questions.text: You notice your spouse seems quieter than usual, nothing dramatic, just slightly withdrawn. They have not said anything is wrong. What do you do?

options.text: I go to them and gently ask what is going on, noticing that something seems off
options.outcomeLabel: You initiate emotional check-ins

genderInsight.male: Noticing your wife's quietness and going to her shows emotional emotional awareness that many husbands lack. You're not waiting for her to ask for help — you're reading the room and initiating. This is relational leadership.
genderInsight.female: Initiating a check-in when your husband is withdrawn shows you refuse to let distance grow silently. Many wives wait for him to come to them — your willingness to bridge the gap first is powerful.

options.text: I give them space and wait for them to come to me. I do not want to push if they are not ready
options.outcomeLabel: You respect space but stay passive

genderInsight.male: Giving space when your wife is withdrawn can be wisdom or avoidance — the difference is whether you come back. If giving space means waiting indefinitely for her to come to you, it's not respect; it's passivity.
genderInsight.female: Respecting his space while staying emotionally available is a valid approach. The growth edge is making sure 'giving space' has an endpoint — otherwise it becomes permanent distance.

options.text: Notice it, but stay quiet. Unsure how to bring it up without it turning into something heavy
options.outcomeLabel: You notice issues but avoid addressing them

genderInsight.male: Noticing but not engaging means you're emotionally aware but relationally passive. Your wife needs more than a husband who sees her — she needs one who reaches for her when she's pulling away.
genderInsight.female: Seeing something is off but avoiding the conversation usually means past attempts went badly. The fear of making it worse keeps you both stuck in unaddressed distance.

options.text: Probably would not notice. We do not track each other's emotional states that closely anymore
options.outcomeLabel: You're emotionally unaware of your spouse

genderInsight.male: Not tracking your wife's emotional state means you've disconnected from the most important monitoring system in your marriage. If you can't tell when she's off, you won't catch problems until they're crises.
genderInsight.female: If you wouldn't notice your husband withdrawing, the emotional channel between you has gone quiet. This isn't about attention span — it's about whether you're still tuned in to each other.

genderVariant.male: You notice your wife seems quieter than usual, nothing dramatic, just slightly withdrawn. She has not said anything is wrong. What do you do?
genderVariant.female: You notice your husband seems quieter than usual, nothing dramatic, just slightly withdrawn. He has not said anything is wrong. What do you do?

questions.text: Something happened today that affected you, good or bad. You walk through the door and your spouse is there. What is your instinct?

options.text: I go straight to them. They are the first person I want to tell. I know they will care about what I am feeling
options.outcomeLabel: Your spouse is the first person you turn to

genderInsight.male: Your wife being the first person you want to tell — good news or bad — means she's still your emotional home. Many husbands stop sharing over the years without realizing it. Your instinct to go to her first is a sign of deep connection.
genderInsight.female: Going straight to your husband when something moves you means he's still your person. This instinct to share — not just coexist — is the heartbeat of emotional intimacy.

options.text: Sharing, but the edited version, enough for connection without risking their disengagement from the full story
options.outcomeLabel: You share selectively for self-protection

genderInsight.male: Editing what you share means you've started managing your wife's response rather than trusting her with the full story. Ask yourself what you're protecting — her, or yourself from her reaction.
genderInsight.female: Sharing the summary version but not the real version means something has made full honesty feel risky. When did you start filtering? That moment often reveals what changed.

options.text: Keeping it to myself. A friend or my own head feels like a safer place to process than bringing it to my spouse
options.outcomeLabel: Your spouse is not your go-to person

genderInsight.male: If your friend hears your real thoughts before your wife does, your emotional intimacy has reversed. A marriage where the husband outsources his inner life to friends isn't broken — but it's hollowing out.
genderInsight.female: Choosing a friend over your husband for emotional processing isn't wrong in itself — but if it's your default, your marriage has lost its position as your primary emotional relationship.

options.text: I do not share things like this anymore. We have stopped being each other's emotional landing place
options.outcomeLabel: Emotional sharing has stopped between you

genderInsight.male: Stopping emotional sharing entirely means you've given up on being known by your wife. This is often the last stage before emotional divorce — the marriage continues functionally but the connection is gone.
genderInsight.female: When you no longer bring anything real to your husband — not the good, not the bad — the marriage has become a logistical arrangement. Rebuilding this requires intentional reconnection, probably with professional help.

questions.text: Your child (or a child in your care) pushes a boundary in front of both of you. In the moment, what happens between you and your spouse?

options.text: We are mostly on the same page. We handle it together, or one leads and the other supports without undermining
options.outcomeLabel: You present a united parenting front

genderInsight.male: United parenting means your children see their parents as a team, not two separate authorities to play against each other. As a father, supporting your wife's decisions in the moment — even when you'd do it differently — builds family stability.
genderInsight.female: A united front in parenting means your children feel secure in consistent boundaries. This requires you and your husband to have done the behind-the-scenes work of aligning your approaches.

options.text: We try to be united but sometimes contradict each other in the moment. We debrief afterward
options.outcomeLabel: You react but then repair

genderInsight.male: Contradicting each other in the moment then debriefing later is workable but confusing for kids. The fix isn't agreement on everything — it's a rule: support in the moment, discuss in private.
genderInsight.female: Reactive disagreement followed by private repair shows good intentions but imperfect execution. The child sees the contradiction; the repair happens where they can't. Consider agreeing on a 'default parent' rule.

options.text: One of us takes over and the other steps back or disagrees. It creates confusion for the child and tension between us
options.outcomeLabel: You're divided on who leads the home

genderInsight.male: If one of you takes over while the other steps back, your children are learning that parenting is a power contest, not a partnership. As a father, this often looks like either dominating or deferring entirely.
genderInsight.female: Split authority teaches children to seek the lenient parent, which divides you further. If you and your husband can't parent together, the child pays the price.

options.text: Parenting moments often become arguments between us. The child's behavior triggers our own unresolved issues
options.outcomeLabel: Parenting triggers conflict between you

genderInsight.male: When parenting triggers marital conflict, the child becomes both the subject and the audience of your disagreement. Children who witness this internalize blame. Protecting them requires protecting your parenting alliance.
genderInsight.female: Parenting becoming a battlefield means the child's behavior is less the issue than how you and your husband relate under pressure. This needs couples work, not parenting tips.

questions.text: One of you is going through a genuinely hard season: a health scare, career crisis, or the loss of someone close. How does faith show up between you as a couple during this time?

options.text: We pray together, process it through our faith, and lean into God as a couple. This is when our shared faith is most real
options.outcomeLabel: Your shared faith activates under pressure

genderInsight.male: Shared faith activating under pressure is the truest test of spiritual partnership. As a husband, leading your wife to prayer during crisis — not just handling the logistics — is transformative spiritual leadership.
genderInsight.female: Turning to God together in crisis means faith is functional in your marriage, not ornamental. This shared reliance is the deepest form of spiritual intimacy.

options.text: We each turn to God individually. Faith is important to both of us but we have not built the habit of processing it together
options.outcomeLabel: Your faith lives side by side, not together

genderInsight.male: Parallel faith during crisis means you're each going to God separately rather than together. As a husband, simply saying 'can we pray about this together?' bridges that gap.
genderInsight.female: Individual faith is real, but shared faith in crisis hits differently. If you've never prayed together through a hard season, you've missed one of the most bonding experiences marriage offers.

options.text: One of us leans into faith and the other pulls away. Our spiritual responses to crisis do not match
options.outcomeLabel: You experience spiritual mismatch in crisis

genderInsight.male: If your wife turns to faith while you pull away in crisis — or vice versa — you're coping in opposite directions. This spiritual mismatch can feel like abandonment at the worst possible time.
genderInsight.female: One leaning in while the other pulls away creates spiritual loneliness during the season you most need each other. This mismatch is worth discussing during calm, not during crisis.

options.text: Faith does not really come up. In hard times we rely on practical solutions, and spiritual connection feels disconnected
options.outcomeLabel: Your faith is absent during hardship

genderInsight.male: Faith absent in hardship means your marriage only has human resources during superhuman challenges. As a husband, you don't need to have answers — you need to be willing to seek them together with God.
genderInsight.female: Relying only on practical solutions during crisis leaves out the most important resource available to a Christian marriage. Faith doesn't eliminate hard seasons — it provides a foundation to endure them together.

questions.text: An extended family member (in-law, parent, sibling) repeatedly oversteps a boundary in your marriage or home. How do you and your spouse handle it?

options.text: The spouse whose family it is takes the lead in setting the boundary. We protect our marriage as a unit
options.outcomeLabel: You set boundaries with marriage first

genderInsight.male: Taking the lead in setting boundaries with your own family protects your wife from being the 'bad guy.' As a husband, your mother or father respecting your marriage starts with you enforcing it.
genderInsight.female: Marriage-first boundaries mean your husband puts your relationship above his family of origin when it counts. If you're the one setting boundaries with his family, the dynamic is backwards.

options.text: We agree it is a problem but struggle to confront it. One of us is protective of their family
options.outcomeLabel: You avoid conflict with extended family

genderInsight.male: Struggling to confront your own family is one of the most common marriage stressors for men. Your wife needs to know you'll choose her over keeping the peace with your parents.
genderInsight.female: If your husband won't confront his own family, you feel unprotected — and you're right to. But pushing him may not work; helping him see the cost of inaction often does.

options.text: It is become a recurring fight between us. The outside interference is straining our marriage
options.outcomeLabel: Outside pressure is pulling your marriage apart

genderInsight.male: External family pressure becoming a recurring fight means the boundary hasn't been set clearly enough — or one of you keeps caving. As a husband, your marriage must be the primary loyalty.
genderInsight.female: In-law interference straining your marriage means the boundary is being discussed between you instead of being enforced with them. The conversation needs to shift to the right audience.

options.text: My spouse sides with their family over me. I feel like I am competing for priority in my own marriage
options.outcomeLabel: You experience conflicting priorities between spouse and extended family

genderInsight.male: If your wife feels she's competing with your mother for priority, your family-of-origin loyalty is threatening your marriage. A man who can't prioritize his wife over his parents hasn't fully left and cleaved.
genderInsight.female: Feeling like you come second to his family is one of the most painful positions in marriage. You deserve to be your husband's primary loyalty — and Scripture supports this ('leave and cleave').
